species.name: Inkcarp
species.description: A carp whose fins leave trails of ink in the water.
species.lore: Inkcarp write. Their ink trails form characters that scholars copy to practise calligraphy. Most of what they write is about waterfalls.

folklore_sources.tradition: The carp that strives to leap the Dragon Gate.

species.name: Scrollfin
species.description: A long carp with fins like unrolled scrolls covered in flowing script.
species.lore: Scrollfins gather below waterfalls and read aloud the characters their younger kin have written. Each one is sure it will leap the Gate next year.

folklore_sources.tradition: The carp that strives to leap the Dragon Gate.

species.name: Lantern Moth
species.description: A moth with papery wings that glow like a lit lantern.
species.lore: Lantern Moths gather at festivals and settle on unlit lanterns until they glow. Children count them for luck.

folklore_sources.tradition: Lantern festivals — the Lantern Festival in China, Hội An's lantern nights in Vietnam and Yi Peng in northern Thailand.

species.name: Lampwing
species.description: A great moth whose wingspan is patterned like a painted festival lantern.
species.lore: A Lampwing leads lost travellers home by flying just ahead of them. It never lands until they are safe.

folklore_sources.tradition: Lantern festivals — the Lantern Festival in China, Hội An's lantern nights in Vietnam and Yi Peng in northern Thailand.

species.name: Paddy Heron
species.description: A slender white heron that stands motionless in flooded rice fields.
species.lore: Farmers say a Paddy Heron in the field means a good planting. It can stand still from dawn until noon.

folklore_sources.tradition: Herons and egrets in ink painting as symbols of patience and purity.

species.name: Stiltsage
species.description: A tall, grey-plumed heron with a crest like a scholar's cap.
species.lore: Stiltsages are said to have read every scroll ever dropped in a river. They answer questions by tapping the water.

folklore_sources.tradition: Herons and egrets in ink painting as symbols of patience and purity.

species.name: Teacup Tortoise
species.description: A tiny tortoise whose shell looks exactly like a glazed teacup.
species.lore: Teahouses keep one on the counter for luck. Guests swear that tea poured beside it never goes cold.

folklore_sources.tradition: The tortoise as a symbol of longevity, and the tea ceremony's patience.

species.name: Teahouse Tortoise
species.description: A great tortoise carrying a miniature tiled pavilion on its shell.
species.lore: Small beasts shelter in the pavilion on its back. It walks one step an hour and has never been late for anything that mattered.

folklore_sources.tradition: The tortoise as a symbol of longevity, and the tea ceremony's patience.

species.name: Fox Ember
species.description: A slim red fox whose tail tip flickers like a candle flame.
species.lore: Travellers see lights bobbing along country roads at night and know a Fox Ember is out walking. Following the lights is a bad idea.

folklore_sources.tradition: Kitsunebi, the "fox-fires" — lights seen on country roads at night and blamed on foxes.

species.name: Pyrebrush
species.description: A fox with a great brush tail of living flame that never burns what it touches.
species.lore: A Pyrebrush leads processions of fox-fires along hillside paths on winter nights. It is not unfriendly, but it does enjoy watching people get lost.

folklore_sources.tradition: Kitsunebi, the "fox-fires" — lights seen on country roads at night and blamed on foxes.

species.name: Granary Mouse
species.description: A tiny brown mouse with a pouch of rice always tucked in its cheeks.
species.lore: A granary with mice is a granary with grain. Farmers count them, and grow uneasy when there are none.

folklore_sources.tradition: Mice and rats as signs of a full granary and household plenty.

species.name: Ricewarden
species.description: A plump, alert mouse that patrols granaries and drives off pests.
species.lore: A Ricewarden keeps exactly one grain in ten and guards the rest from everything else. Farmers think this is a fair price.

folklore_sources.tradition: Mice and rats as signs of a full granary and household plenty.

species.name: Wallowcalf
species.description: A dark, round-bellied buffalo calf that is never more than a step from water.
species.lore: Wallowcalves follow farm children to school and wait outside, knee-deep in the nearest paddy.

folklore_sources.tradition: The water buffalo (carabao, kerbau, trâu) as a partner in rice farming, honoured in harvest festivals across the region.

species.name: Wallowhorn
species.description: A massive water buffalo with sweeping crescent horns and a coat of drying river mud.
species.lore: A Wallowhorn ploughs a field without a driver if it likes the farmer. Villages hold races for them after the harvest.

folklore_sources.tradition: The water buffalo (carabao, kerbau, trâu) as a partner in rice farming, honoured in harvest festivals across the region.

species.name: Mistkit
species.description: A small spotted cat with cloud-shaped markings that seem to drift.
species.lore: Mistkits are only ever glimpsed in fog. Hunters say that if you can see one clearly, it has decided to be seen.

folklore_sources.tradition: The clouded leopard of mountain forests, rarely seen and often said to be a spirit of the mist.

species.name: Cloudpelt
species.description: A long-tailed tree cat whose coat is a moving map of clouds.
species.lore: A Cloudpelt can climb down a tree head-first and hang by its hind paws. It watches villages from the canopy for years before it ever comes down.

folklore_sources.tradition: The clouded leopard of mountain forests, rarely seen and often said to be a spirit of the mist.

species.name: Burrbun
species.description: A small brown rabbit whose fur is always tangled with burrs.
species.lore: Burrbuns spread seeds wherever they go. A meadow full of brambles probably has a Burrbun to thank.

folklore_sources.tradition: The hare as a quick-witted survivor in countryside tales.

species.name: Bramblehare
species.description: A long-legged hare that weaves through thorn thickets without a scratch.
species.lore: A Bramblehare leads pursuers into the thorns and out the other side, where it waits, patiently, for them to untangle themselves.

folklore_sources.tradition: The hare as a quick-witted survivor in countryside tales.

species.name: Callgecko
species.description: A spotted gecko whose loud two-note call echoes through the house at night.
species.lore: Families count a Callgecko's calls. An odd number means yes, an even number no, and seven in a row means a baby is on the way.

folklore_sources.tradition: The tokay gecko's call, counted aloud for luck or answers in households across the region.

species.name: Eavesgecko
species.description: A large gecko that clings to rafters and guards the household from pests.
species.lore: An Eavesgecko in the rafters keeps away insects, snakes and bad luck. Nobody evicts one; it would be like evicting a grandparent.

folklore_sources.tradition: The tokay gecko's call, counted aloud for luck or answers in households across the region.

species.name: Packfoal
species.description: A shaggy, short-legged foal with a bell on its halter.
species.lore: Packfoals walk beside the caravan before they are old enough to carry anything. The bell is so the caravan always knows where they are.

folklore_sources.tradition: The Tea Horse Road, where caravans of ponies carried tea one way and horses and salt the other across high mountain passes.

species.name: Saltroad Pony
species.description: A tough mountain pony laden with bricks of tea and blocks of salt.
species.lore: A Saltroad Pony knows every pass between the Hours and walks them without a guide. Caravan masters trust its judgement over any map.

folklore_sources.tradition: The Tea Horse Road, where caravans of ponies carried tea one way and horses and salt the other across high mountain passes.

species.name: Crag Kid
species.description: A small dark goat-antelope that bounds up cliffs on its first day.
species.lore: Crag Kids are born on ledges and learn to climb before they learn to walk on flat ground.

folklore_sources.tradition: The serow, a mountain goat-antelope of steep forests, admired for its surefootedness.

species.name: Cliffserow
species.description: A shaggy, maned goat-antelope with short spiked horns.
species.lore: A Cliffserow stands on one ledge its entire life. Climbers who reach it leave a pinch of salt, and it lets them pass.

folklore_sources.tradition: The serow, a mountain goat-antelope of steep forests, admired for its surefootedness.

species.name: Duskloris
species.description: A round-eyed loris that moves with dreamlike slowness.
species.lore: A Duskloris moves so slowly that people forget it is there. Its bite carries a sleepy venom, which it uses only when it has been very rudely treated.

folklore_sources.tradition: The slow loris, a shy night primate surrounded by many local beliefs about luck and misfortune.

species.name: Moonloris
species.description: A silver-masked loris whose huge eyes reflect moonlight.
species.lore: A Moonloris sees in the dark as others see at noon. It never hurries, and it has never once been caught unprepared.

folklore_sources.tradition: The slow loris, a shy night primate surrounded by many local beliefs about luck and misfortune.

species.name: Whistlepup
species.description: A rust-red pup that whistles instead of barking.
species.lore: Whistlepups are raised by the whole pack. A lost one whistles, and every adult within a valley answers.

folklore_sources.tradition: The dhole, a wild dog that hunts in packs and calls to its packmates with whistles.

species.name: Redwhistle
species.description: A lean red wild dog with a dark bushy tail and a piercing whistle.
species.lore: A pack of Redwhistles hunts in perfect silence, then whistles all at once. Keepers who bond with one often find the rest of the pack following them home.

folklore_sources.tradition: The dhole, a wild dog that hunts in packs and calls to its packmates with whistles.

species.name: Bristlet
species.description: A striped piglet with a tuft of whiskers like a tiny beard.
species.lore: Bristlets follow fruiting trees with their herd, walking for weeks to reach the next feast.

folklore_sources.tradition: The bearded pig and its long seasonal migrations following fruiting forests.

species.name: Bristleboar
species.description: A long-snouted boar with a magnificent bristly beard.
species.lore: When the forest fruits, Bristleboar herds arrive within days from nowhere anyone can explain. Villages plan their own harvests by their arrival.

folklore_sources.tradition: The bearded pig and its long seasonal migrations following fruiting forests.

species.name: Chirpling
species.description: A tiny green cricket with a surprisingly loud chirp.
species.lore: Chirplings sing on autumn evenings. Those who hear one on the first cool night say the summer heat has broken.

folklore_sources.tradition: Keeping singing crickets for their song, in carved gourds in China and small cages in Japan, as a sign of autumn.

species.name: Bellcricket
species.description: A bronze cricket whose song rings like a struck temple bell.
species.lore: Bellcrickets were once kept in carved gourds for their song. A kind Keeper set one free, and it followed her for the rest of her life, singing. They have chosen Keepers ever since.

folklore_sources.tradition: Keeping singing crickets for their song, in carved gourds in China and small cages in Japan, as a sign of autumn.
